concept.name: Two-Phase Commit

relationships.description: Connects Two-Phase Commit to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) coordinates an atomic all-or-nothing transaction across independent shards or services by splitting execution into a durable `PREPARE` voting round followed by a `COMMIT` or `ABORT` decision.
spark.keyTakeaway: 2PC guarantees atomicity across distributed participants, but a coordinator crash during the `PREPARE` window leaves participants blocked holding locks until the coordinator recovers.

concept.whyItMatters: Distributed databases (Google Spanner, CockroachDB, Citus) and XA transaction managers use 2PC whenever a single business operation must atomically update records living on different shards or resource managers without partial writes.
whenToUse: Cross-shard ACID transactions inside a single distributed database (e.g., transferring funds between Shard A and Shard B in Spanner or Citus) where participants are backed by Raft/Paxos.
Legacy enterprise integrations requiring XA-compliant `PREPARE`/`COMMIT` across a relational DB and a message broker (IBM MQ, ActiveMQ) in low-throughput back-office flows.
Short-lived (<50 ms) distributed state transitions inside a single datacenter with high-availability replicated coordinators.
whenNotToUse: Cross-microservice workflows spanning independent teams, external payment gateways (Stripe), or third-party APIs; use the Saga pattern or Transactional Outbox + CDC instead.
Geo-distributed multi-region writes with high WAN RTT (100–200 ms) unless latency is acceptable or parallel-commit optimizations (CockroachDB) are used.
High-throughput event pipelines (>50k TPS) where synchronous `fsync` round-trips and cross-node lock holding collapse concurrency.
keyPoints: Phase 1 (Prepare): The coordinator sends `PREPARE` to all participants; each participant acquires locks, writes undo/redo records to its local WAL, `fsync`s to disk, and replies `YES` (or `NO`).
Phase 2 (Commit/Abort): Only if *every* participant votes `YES` does the coordinator durably log `COMMIT` to its own WAL and send `COMMIT` to all participants; any `NO` or timeout triggers `ABORT`.
Once a participant logs `PREPARED` and votes `YES`, it surrenders unilateral autonomy—it cannot abort or commit on its own and must hold locks until the coordinator decides.
2PC is a **blocking protocol**: if the coordinator crashes after participants vote `YES` (and before sending `COMMIT`/`ABORT`), participants remain stuck in-doubt until the coordinator restarts.
Modern NewSQL systems (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB) eliminate single-node coordinator blocking by replicating both the coordinator state and each shard via Paxos/Raft.

examples.title: Cross-Shard Ledger Transfer in PostgreSQL/Citus
examples.scenario: A banking core splits accounts across two PostgreSQL shards (`shard_a` and `shard_b`) and executes a $500 transfer using PostgreSQL `PREPARE TRANSACTION` / `COMMIT PREPARED`.
examples.outcome: Citus issues `PREPARE TRANSACTION 'tx_9182'` to both shards. Both `fsync` their WAL and return `OK`. Citus logs the commit decision and issues `COMMIT PREPARED 'tx_9182'`. If `shard_b` fails validation during prepare, Citus issues `ROLLBACK PREPARED` on `shard_a`, leaving zero partial transfers.

examples.title: Google Spanner 2PC Over Paxos Groups
examples.scenario: A global inventory update spans two Paxos-replicated splits in different zones.
examples.outcome: Because the 2PC coordinator itself is a Raft/Paxos group rather than a single machine, a coordinator leader crash triggers a <10s Paxos leader election; the new leader reads the replicated `COMMIT`/`ABORT` log and unblocks participants automatically.

tradeOffs.pro: 2PC provides strict serializable isolation—no intermediate uncommitted state is ever visible to concurrent readers.
tradeOffs.con: 2PC holds locks across network round-trips and blocks on coordinator failure, whereas Sagas release locks immediately and scale across external APIs.

tradeOffs.pro: 2PC updates two systems synchronously in one request-response cycle.
tradeOffs.con: Outbox + Debezium avoids distributed locks entirely, delivering higher throughput and availability at the cost of eventual consistency.

tradeOffs.pro: Presumed-Abort skips synchronous `fsync` of abort records on the coordinator, saving disk I/O on failed transactions.
tradeOffs.con: Requires participants to treat missing coordinator state as an abort, adding protocol state-machine subtleties.

failureModes.name: Coordinator Crash Leaving In-Doubt Locks
failureModes.description: The coordinator dies after participants flush `PREPARED` to WAL. Participants hold row/table locks indefinitely, piling up blocked queries across the cluster.
failureModes.mitigation: Replicate the coordinator state via Raft/Paxos, or set strict `max_prepared_transactions` monitoring with runbooks for manual heuristic resolution only as a last resort.

failureModes.name: Network Partition & Heuristic Commit Split-Brain
failureModes.description: An operator manually runs `COMMIT PREPARED` on Shard A during a partition while the coordinator later decides `ABORT` on Shard B, corrupting cross-shard invariants.
failureModes.mitigation: Never mix automatic 2PC with manual heuristic overrides unless the entire transaction outcome is verified across all participants.

failureModes.name: Tail-Latency Amplification (Straggler Participant)
failureModes.description: A single slow participant (GC pause, noisy-neighbor disk `fsync`) delays Phase 1 `PREPARE`, forcing every other healthy participant to hold locks longer.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce aggressive Phase 1 prepare timeouts (e.g., 200–500 ms) so stalled transactions abort quickly and release locks.

failureModes.name: Forgotten Prepared Transactions Exhausting Slots
failureModes.description: Orphaned `PREPARE TRANSACTION` entries in PostgreSQL hold back the `xmin` horizon, blocking `VACUUM` and causing severe table bloat.
failureModes.mitigation: Alert on `pg_prepared_xacts` age > 60 seconds and enforce automated coordinator reaper jobs.

commonMistakes: Using XA/2PC across HTTP microservices over the public internet instead of idempotent Sagas or Outbox patterns.
Omitting `fsync` on the participant's `PREPARED` WAL record—if a participant crashes and forgets its `YES` vote after the coordinator commits, atomicity is broken.
Confusing 2PC (an atomic commit protocol) with Raft/Paxos (a consensus protocol for replicating a single state machine); 2PC requires consensus on the coordinator to be non-blocking.
Assuming 3-Phase Commit (3PC) solves all 2PC blocking in production—3PC still fails under network partitions (FLP impossibility) and is rarely used.
Ignoring `max_prepared_transactions` limits in PostgreSQL (default is `0`, disabling 2PC).

sections.content:
## The idea

When data lives on two independent nodes (say, `Shard A` and `Shard B`), a local ACID commit on `Shard A` cannot be rolled back if `Shard B` crashes a millisecond later. **Two-Phase Commit (2PC)** solves this by introducing a **Coordinator** and splitting commitment into two durable steps:

1. **Phase 1 (Voting / Prepare)**: Can every participant guarantee it can commit?
2. **Phase 2 (Decision / Commit)**: Now that every participant has durably promised, execute the commit (or abort if anyone said no).

The core invariant is **irrevocability**: once a participant writes `PREPARED` to its Write-Ahead Log and votes `YES`, it cannot unilaterally roll back—even if it reboots.

## Concrete walkthrough

Walk through transferring $100 from `Account 1` (Shard A) to `Account 2` (Shard B) under transaction `tx_42`:

1. **Phase 1 (`PREPARE`)**: The coordinator sends `PREPARE tx_42` to Shard A and Shard B. Shard A checks `balance >= 100`, acquires an exclusive row lock on `Account 1`, writes the redo/undo log plus `PREPARE tx_42` to disk (`fsync`), and replies `VOTE_YES`. Shard B locks `Account 2`, `fsync`s `PREPARE tx_42`, and replies `VOTE_YES`.
2. **Coordinator Decision**: Having received `VOTE_YES` from all participants, the coordinator writes `COMMIT tx_42` to its own WAL (`fsync`). At this exact instant, the transaction is logically committed.
3. **Phase 2 (`COMMIT`)**: The coordinator sends `COMMIT tx_42` to Shard A and Shard B. Each participant writes `COMMIT` to its WAL, releases the row locks on `Account 1` and `Account 2`, and sends `ACK` back so the coordinator can garbage-collect `tx_42`.

sections.content:
## Why vanilla 2PC blocks

Consider what happens if the coordinator crashes right after Shard A and Shard B vote `YES`, but before it sends `COMMIT` (or `ABORT`).

Shard A cannot abort `tx_42` because the coordinator might have logged `COMMIT` and already told Shard B to commit. Conversely, Shard A cannot commit because the coordinator might have crashed *before* logging `COMMIT` and will abort on recovery. Therefore, Shard A is **blocked** in the `PREPARED` state, holding exclusive locks on `Account 1` until the coordinator recovers (or an administrator intervenes). Note that participant-to-participant queries cannot safely resolve this if *all* participants are uncertain.

## Distributed atomicity patterns compared

| Pattern | Isolation Level | Availability on Coordinator Crash | Latency Overhead | Best Fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Single-Node 2PC (XA) | Serializable / Snapshot | **Blocks** until coordinator recovers | 2 RTT + 3 sequential `fsync`s | Monolithic DBs or legacy XA |
| Replicated 2PC (Spanner / CockroachDB) | Serializable | **Non-blocking** (Raft/Paxos failover) | 2 RTT (1 RTT w/ Parallel Commits) | Distributed SQL databases |
| Saga (Orchestrated / Choreographed) | Read Uncommitted (dirty reads) | Non-blocking (compensating actions) | $N$ async hops | Cross-service business workflows |
| Transactional Outbox + CDC | Local ACID + Eventual | Non-blocking | 1 local `fsync` + async CDC lag | Event-driven microservices (Kafka/Debezium) |

## Failure modes

In production, 2PC failures center on **lock duration** and **orphaned prepared state**:

- **Prepared transaction leaks**: If a client/coordinator disconnects permanently, prepared transactions linger in `pg_prepared_xacts` (PostgreSQL) or InnoDB `XA RECOVER`, holding locks and blocking garbage collection (`VACUUM`).
- **Cascading timeout storms**: A slow disk on one shard causes Phase 1 to stall; meanwhile, incoming transactions queue behind the locked rows held by `PREPARED` transactions, exhausting connection pools across all shards.

## How modern systems make 2PC fast

Modern distributed databases retain 2PC's strong isolation while fixing its latency and availability flaws:

1. **Consensus-backed Participants & Coordinator**: Every shard and the transaction record itself are Raft/Paxos groups, eliminating single-point-of-failure blocking.
2. **Parallel Commits (CockroachDB)**: Instead of waiting sequentially for `PREPARE` to finish before writing `COMMIT`, CockroachDB writes a `STAGING` transaction record in parallel with intent writes, cutting commit latency from 2 consensus RTTs down to 1 RTT.
3. **Read-Only Optimization**: Participants that only read data (no writes) skip Phase 2 entirely by replying `READ_ONLY` in Phase 1.

## Practical checklist

- Never use 2PC across external third-party APIs or independent microservice boundaries; use Outbox + idempotent consumers or Sagas.
- If using PostgreSQL XA (`PREPARE TRANSACTION`), set alerts on `pg_prepared_xacts` count and age (>30s) to prevent `VACUUM` stalls.
- Replicate the coordinator state (via Raft/Paxos or a HA database) so a single machine failure never leaves locks stranded.
- Keep 2PC transactions short and bounded—never perform network RPCs to external services or user prompts between `PREPARE` and `COMMIT`.
- Enforce idempotent Phase 2 `COMMIT`/`ABORT` retries with exponential backoff until every participant acknowledges.

interviewProblems.title: Two-Phase Commit
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Two-Phase Commit. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) coordinates an atomic all-or-nothing transaction across independent shards or services by splitting execution into a durable `PREPARE` voting round followed by a `COMMIT` or `ABORT` decision.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Participant: Shard A applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Participant: Shard B.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Participant: Shard B experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Replicate the coordinator state via Raft/Paxos, or set strict `max_prepared_transactions` monitoring with runbooks for manual heuristic resolution only as a last resort.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: 2PC guarantees atomicity across distributed participants, but a coordinator crash during the `PREPARE` window leaves participants blocked holding locks until the coordinator recovers.
Avoid trap: Using XA/2PC across HTTP microservices over the public internet instead of idempotent Sagas or Outbox patterns.
Avoid trap: Omitting `fsync` on the participant's `PREPARED` WAL record—if a participant crashes and forgets its `YES` vote after the coordinator commits, atomicity is broken.

When to reach for it: Cross-shard ACID transactions inside a single distributed database (e.g., transferring funds between Shard A and Shard B in Spanner or Citus) where participants are backed by Raft/Paxos.
When to reach for it: Legacy enterprise integrations requiring XA-compliant `PREPARE`/`COMMIT` across a relational DB and a message broker (IBM MQ, ActiveMQ) in low-throughput back-office flows.

putItTogether.title: Putting Two Phase Commit Together
putItTogether.summary: 2PC guarantees atomicity across distributed participants, but a coordinator crash during the `PREPARE` window leaves participants blocked holding locks until the coordinator recovers.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Two Phase Commit before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Citus issues `PREPARE TRANSACTION 'tx_9182'` to both shards. Both `fsync` their WAL and return `OK`. Citus logs the commit decision and issues `COMMIT PREPARED 'tx_9182'`. If `shard_b` fails validation during prepare, Citus issues `ROLLBACK PREPARED` on `shard_a`, leaving zero partial transfers.
